Explain the problem with the molecular scans of the shroud of Turin

The problem isn't one bad scan — it's that every molecular result on the Shroud is hostage to *sampling*, and nobody's allowed to take a fresh one. Here's the shape of it:

**1. The 1988 radiocarbon date (1260–1390 AD) — the famous medieval verdict.** The sample came from a single corner strip — the most-handled, most-contaminated edge of the cloth, and one that textile experts argue was invisibly rewoven after damage. Chemist Ray Rogers showed in 2005 that the C14 sample area was chemically distinct from the main cloth (different vanillin/lignin content). Worse, re-analyses of the raw 1988 data found a ~200-year age *gradient* across just 7 cm of sample — younger toward the cloth's center — which shouldn't exist in a homogeneous sample and, extrapolated, gets absurd fast. Add five centuries of candle smoke, the 1532 fire, water damage, and bacterial colonization in the fiber interstices, and C14 was always going to struggle.

**2. The "it's 2,000 years old" molecular dates — equally shaky from the other side.** De Caro's 2022 WAXS study (X-ray scattering measuring cellulose degradation) matched the fibers to 1st-century Masada linen. Problems: the sample was 0.5 × 1 mm with disputed provenance, the method is non-standard and unvalidated for dating textiles, and the same pair (Fanti & De Caro) rolled out *four* separate novel dating methods between 2014 and 2022, all landing pro-authenticity — they're sindonologists, researchers working from a believing stance. A related 2018 De Caro WAXS paper was retracted by PLOS One over insufficient controls and fiber provenance. A 2025 review judged all these challenges to the 1988 dating insufficient.

**3. The blood chemistry never converged.** McCrone found iron oxide and vermilion — artist's pigment, no blood. Heller and Adler found heme and proteins consistent with real blood. They were reading different tape-lifts from different spots, so it's two labs describing two different samples and calling it the same object.

**4. The structural trap.** The Church restricts new sampling, so the entire field argues over the same crumbs: 1978 STURP tapes, 1988 corner cuttings, millimeter fragments of murky origin. The one experiment that would settle it — fresh multi-site sampling with modern C14 — is exactly what's not permitted, which the 2025 review explicitly called for as the next logical step.

So: the medieval date may have dated a repair, the ancient dates rest on a millimeter of fiber from true believers using bespoke methods, and the blood work is two datasets talking past each other. The scans aren't the problem. The *material* is — contaminated, corner-cut, and off-limits.

Is American poverty at its lowest point

Yes, by the official Census measure: the 2025 poverty rate fell to **10.2%**, the lowest since the series began in 1959 — about 34.5 million people below the line. Child poverty (13.4%) and Hispanic poverty (13.9%) also hit historic lows.

Two caveats: 10.2% is the lowest published rate, but not statistically different from 2019's 10.5%. And the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure — which counts tax credits, SNAP, housing aid, and subtracts medical/work expenses — was higher at 13.1% and essentially flat. The official measure just compares pretax cash income to a national threshold, so "lowest point" depends on which yardstick you trust.
